The narrow-gauge line from Pell to Tarsel climbs nine hundred metres in fourteen kilometres, on rails and curves its builders cut into the mountainside. The Hollin came up the valley with the line in 1911, and for more than a century the little steam engine made the climb every morning. Last autumn her boiler cracked beyond mending. This spring a secondhand diesel railcar, bought by the council from a line in the north, does the work, and I rode it up for the first time.

At Gessen, halfway up, the train pauses for four minutes so that cheese from the Gessen farms can be loaded into its rear compartment. Tomas Brede, who keeps the halt, wheels the crates across while Ilse Marran, who drove the Hollin for twenty-six years, waits in the cab. The water tank beside the track has stood dry since October, its iron lined with a white scale left by years of hard water. Above it, goats graze the scree slope.

Beyond the halt, the stone wall below that slope, rebuilt in 2016 and paid for by the council itself, holds the loose rock firmly. Visitors photograph the viaduct over the Lenn gorge from the windows as we cross. The timetable is the same as before: the first train leaves Tarsel at dawn with the farmers' cheese, a trade the timetable is built around, and the visitors come up afterwards. In winter, when the snowploughs keep the road open, the line carries the post as well.

At Tarsel the Hollin stands cold in the shed beside the platform, and the climb will never again be made behind her. I laid my hand on her iron side and thought of the mornings, years ago, when I rode up behind her with her smoke drifting back past the carriage windows and the whole village hearing her whistle at Gessen. The shed was quiet, and the smell of coal had long since gone from it.

passage:
Ostley's open-air pool opened in 1936 beside the Ost, with a diving tower at the deep end and a pike picked out in blue tiles on the basin floor. It closed in 2019, after a winter flood cracked the basin. The swimming club petitioned the council to put the tiles back under the water. Ostley had been four summers without a pool. Of the four designs entered, Teodora Lind's would cost more than two of its rivals, but it could be built in one summer, where every other design needed two.

Engineers found the diving tower unsound, and it was pulled down; a low new board stands at the deep end in its place. The tiles split as they were lifted, and they were crushed with the cracked old basin into the concrete of the new terrace. The floor of the new basin is pale grey, the pumps sit beneath the terrace, and the café by the north gate has walls of timber from the old changing cubicles. The swimming club had hoped to buy the tiles one by one, but the pieces were too small to keep. A flood wall now stands between the basin and the river.

On opening day entry was free, as it was in 1936, before the fees of later decades became a bar to half the town. The swimming club swam the first length, and the children queued for the new board.

In the café hangs a photograph of opening day in 1936: boys crowding the tower, the swimming club posed on its steps, the terrace full in the afternoon sun, the Ost running a few yards from the edge, and the pike dark beneath the surface. Look again at that tower, with a boy caught in mid-air between the top board and the water. When I stand at the deep end now, I still look up for a tower that is gone.

Three generations of Ostley children learned to dive from that tower, and the place where they learned has gone with it. The pike they swam over is in the terrace now, part of the concrete under the town's feet.

For fifty years before this summer, the seven footbridges over the Askel were the colour of wet pavement. Now they are saffron, coral, teal, plum, lime, sky blue and tangerine, the seven colours that won an online vote of residents in the spring. Councillor Mara Varga ran the vote, and the parks crew painted to its results over six weeks.

I knew those bridges before any of this. On winter mornings the grey spans vanished into the river mist, so that walkers seemed to step off the bank into nothing, and on summer nights the concrete held the day's heat long after dark while we sat on the railings. Every spring the inspectors ringed the cracks in coloured chalk, and by June the rain had washed the rings into pale clouds we traced with our fingers. That grey went under the first coat of saffron in July, and the bridges I grew up on went with it.

I come of ferry stock: my grandfather rowed passengers across the Askel until the bridges opened in 1971, and he walked the grey spans every evening of his retirement. The council's leaflet for the project showed the riverbank crowded with visitors holding cameras, and on weekends now they come.

Other plans came and went first. A class at Larch Street School once put forward a scheme matching each bridge to a bus line, so that people could find the right bridge, and in 2019 the city meant to paint every bridge the same green; the vote overtook both. The crew lost a day when the depot misread an order in a mix-up over the coral tins, and they repaired the cracks the inspectors had ringed, at a cost set aside long ago, before any paint went on.

People say the bridges are easier to tell apart now. What I miss is the hour when all seven turned grey together in the dusk and the river seemed to carry them away, and that hour will not come back.

passage:
Every June Kesterby closes Moss Lane to cars and sends its riders two kilometres uphill from the stone bridge, past the old chapel and the war memorial, to the green. Halfway up is a bend named the Knuckle, where for sixty years a hundred metres of cobbled stones rattled every bicycle that crossed them. Last October, the stones having worn beyond repair, the council laid tarmac over the Knuckle, the last stretch of Moss Lane to be covered.

By custom Hettie Varn, the organiser, sounds the handbell for every rider who reaches the green, the last rider as long as the winner. The field included Arlo Maske, eleven times champion, whose first winning time, 9:41 in 1988, is still the record, though he expects some youngster to break it any June now. In May he had asked the engraver in Hollin to keep the cup's next space for a twelfth win of his own. He had lifted sixteen-year-old Jory Penhale's old steel bicycle and called it heavy but fit for any hill.

Arlo led from the stone bridge, past the old chapel and up the Knuckle, and Jory passed him below the war memorial to reach the green in 9:49, a winning time well outside the champion's record. Nell Odrey finished third. By rule every rider still climbs the Knuckle, and Pell's smooth farm track beside it stays gated. I stood at the bend where I have stood for twenty years and heard only the hiss of tyres on tarmac, where for sixty years there had been the clatter of stone.

Afterwards Hettie set a kettle on the ring in the village hall kitchen, as she has after every race, and the older riders crowded round it talking about the line they used to take across the stones, a seam of flatter cobbles on the left, clear of the loose ones, that only Kesterby riders knew.

The hill is as steep as it ever was. What went under the tarmac in October was the sound of the climb and the old riders' knowledge of its stones, and neither will come back.

March 2. Ms. Fenn says contest letters must be typed on a manual typewriter, with a deadline of Friday the thirteenth. The old machine in Gran's attic belonged to a lodger who left it behind decades ago, and Gran says she never once lifted its lid. The carriage had stopped working and refused to budge. Dad, who doubted the whole plan, said I would waste the week on it and should give up while I could. My cousin Juno sided with me.

March 4. Juno came with me to Keel Street and introduced herself to Mr. Ostrow, the old repairman. He said he could remember this model only from catalogues. He offered me forty dollars for it, and when I shook my head he offered sixty, then asked to be told first if I ever changed my mind. In the end he handed me a booklet explaining the machine and refused to let me pay.

March 5. Dad picked up the booklet, meaning to prove me wrong, and read it with me on the porch, spread across the carved stone capital he rescued from the old post office. The carriage had stopped only because a small lever on its side was set to lock. Dad and I found the lever together; on my own I would have forced the carriage and snapped its spring. After that one visit, we never went back to the old repairman.

March 7. Dad oiled the keys himself with the can from the garage, I borrowed a soft brush from Gran, and Ms. Fenn found a spare ribbon at school. Juno watched. I typed my opening sentence, then rolled in a spare sheet and typed a short message to Dad saying the machine runs because he read that booklet with me, and left it on his pillow.

March 9. I posted the letter this morning, four days before the deadline. Juno, who is two years past the contest's age limit, asked what I planned to do with the machine now, and whether it would fit in her bike basket for a week or two. She has never typed a word in her life.
